item.description: When I heard about Anthropic's new ability to distribute apps you write in Claude to other users. They are full featured desktop apps, much the way BonBon is. They come with identity and storage, but not the kind of storage we would need to provide a dead-simple Markdown editor for someone to quickly start publishing on the Markdown web. I tried explaining what we need, to Felix Rieseberg, the Anthropic rep on Twitter, in the form of an open letter from my Claude agent, who I had walked through on the idea. Their ability to share is between two people who are logged onto Claude. We need it to be possible for any document to have an address that can be accessed over the web, ie to be published. For now we're going to have to pursue different approaches, but the Anthropic approach was tantalizing.

item.description: We now have docs for stylesheets and page handlers. We've been saying all along that the reader has control over appearance and code, and this is how that works. Stylesheets are CSS. You can choose a stylesheet from the popup dialog. The change is reflected immediately in the document you're reading. You can download and install stylesheets by copying them into the stylesheets folder. The handlers folder contains JavaScript functions that handle how various file types are rendered in BonBon. We include handlers for .js and .json. They run in a sandbox, so they can't read or change files on your local system, or access the network. All of this is fully explained in docs in the BonBon repo.

item.description: Next focus in bonbon-land is writing. We have a good start on reading with the demo site and the full app for Mac and Linux desktops. Initially writing is going to come from at least two places: 1. WordPress and 2. RSS.chat. But most important are the myriad possible ways people like to write. This is where having open formats and protocols will really pay off. Writing tools can depend on interop, they won't have to blaze their own trail so much. People creating brilliant writing tools like to focus on that, not a dozen different incompatible APIs and limits. How the hell do you get writing to fit into 500 chars on one network, 300 on another, 280 on yet another. And character limits are just the beginning.

item.title: lobste.rs discussion re BonBon
item.description:
A few quick responses to a discussion thread about BonBon.

  1. We definitely do allow the client to control the appearance of writing. That's a very basic principle. I've written about it a lot and it's in the product. We didn't eliminate CSS or JavaScript, we just gave that power to the reader, not the writer.
  2. Why base it on Markdown? Because it's the obvious choice. If there weren't such a universal trust in Markdown, BonBon wouldn't be possible. It's playing the same role as MP3 did in establishing podcasting. And the different dialects aren't a problem, there is a core set of features they agree on. We'll get by.
  3. Jimmv: "But on my phone, clicking the link just gives me a Markdown doc, unrendered. What am I missing?" Grab the URL of the markdown file, go to demo.bonbonweb.org, and paste the url into the text box at the top. You will see a rendered version. It does the same thing as the standalone BonBon app. We realized that to get started, almost no one would have the browser, so we created the demo site that runs inside an HTML-based browser.
  4. Does it have LaTeX for math? No. But you have given me something to look into with Claude Code. Thanks!
  5. Is it possible to make a a Firefox addon that renders Markdown content to HTML? You don't need an add-in, jut follow the instructions for Jimmv above.
  6. "Oh, nice! I've been saying for a while that browsers should have native support for rendering markdown docs, it's nice to see somebody else saying it too!" And we hope the HTML browsers adopt this. As well as Twitter, Facebook, Mastodon, Bluesky, Threads etc. We need to get out of the age of character limits, no titles possible, no editing -- etc etc. This is how writing on the web got destroyed. It was confined to silos that didn't peer with other systems. They wouldn't listen to our ideas so we made the software for them to compete with. ;-)

item.description: A friend asks what's the deal with the dog. Once a very long time ago, when I was living in Silicon Valley, I had a black lab named BonBon. She was a handful, for sure -- and I didn't know anything about training dogs, so she was also pretty wild. But she had the biggest heart and was totally devoted to me, and was pretty much my constant companion. Her joy in life was infectuous and memorable. Now I don't want to sound all gushy (go ahead) but BonBon the software which is named after BonBon the pup, gives me that feeling of joy too. I loved the web as much as I ever loved anything, because it blew open the doors on a really fucked up industry run by total children, whose first impulse was to destroy anything they could, even if it wasn't in their way. They did that to the web. But the web, via BonBon, says basically, you can do it. The courage of that little dog, BonBon, with the same name in two different contexts, reminds me that this is right, and it is working.

item.description: Resetting priorities for Day 3 of the life of BonBon. I have gotten messages from friends who are thinking about how to create a Markdown web site of their own. I want to share interesting examples showing how people have done it. So here's the first one. We spent a fair amount of time getting Scripting News to be part of this experiment. We wrote a server app that watches what's going on, via the RSS 2.0 feed. When it sees a new or updated post, it generates a Markdown file and updates the toc.opml file to link it into the chronology of the blog. It also recognizes some custom front matter values, and handles special cases for Markdown itself. For example, an image that appears at the beginning of a paragraph, before anything else, is shown in the right margin, like the beautiful Lab in the right margin. It also has a special syntax for inline images, like the one in this post. There's a general config file alongside toc.opml in the .well-known folder at the top level. Also they can be nested, so you could have a .well-known folder at any level. Anyway all this is to say that we've shared a snapshot of the scripting website in markdown in the BonBon repo. More of these to come, and we want to see new examples from people working on this stuff so we can share them with the community. This like coming up with a platform and sharing developer stories.

item.description: Also, learned that Claude Code can forget to do things when it rebuilds an app for distribution. I found this when I, as a user, did an update and the desktop icon for BonBon was blank. I figured it would take a few hours before the OS straightened it out, but it didn't. We then discovered this flaw. People who think AI tools are perfection are in for a rude awakening. They always forget stuff. It's really irritating, after all it's a freaking computer -- we expect computers to have perfect memory. Maybe someday. So you may not realize that the beautiful Black Lab I've been including in the right margins of posts is also the identity of the product. If you've ever had a Black Lab, as I have, you know that you're getting an extremely loyal, friendly and fun-loving best friend, who demands basically all your time, esp when they're young. What does that portend? Probably nothing, but it makes me smile when I see it.

item.title: BonBon is podcasting for text
item.description:
Four docs developers should download and give to their AI assistants. Then your helper can answer a lot of questions about what BonBon does now, and what it will never do.

  • Claude Code handoff document for BonBon.
  • Charter. The philosophy of the Markdown web and BonBon.
  • Textcasting explainer.
  • Rules for standards-makers. A frequently cited howto I wrote in 2017 about what works and doesn't in making interop via standards.

We put a lot of thought into how this new web should start and how it can preserve its independence in the future. The key is user expectations, and you don't need a lot of users to set the DNA for a new movement. In this case, we're clear on the power of writers and readers. The platform respects both equally.

  • The reader controls the font, colors, basically how the writing is presented. This idea came from a feature on my iPad, where I as a reader can remove everything but the writing from a web page. I miss it when I'm working on a desktop or laptop.
  • The writer is given a rational writing platform without the ridiculous limits of today's social networks. You don't have to fit your writing into 140, 280, 300 or 500 characters. You can give your document a title, or not, it's up to you to decide if your writing needs one. You can use simple styles, and link from a word or phrase to another location on the web. A consistent set of rules on all platforms is the beginning of real interop

As a writer, when you adopt BonBon, you're sending a clear message to the writing world such as it exists today, that you want them to interop with the other social networks, the same way podcasting set a standard, and we don't have any silos in that world. None. They can't take root because the users expect to get their radio from "wherever you get podcasts." We're going to be doing the same with writing in the future, which is actually here now. Expectations are key.

I'm proud of podcasting, and totally lament we haven't taken care of text as well. It's not too late to start.

As we used to say on this blog -- Zoooooooom!

item.title: Getting started with BonBon
item.description:
We're finally ready to start building the Markdown web.

  • Here's the BonBon repo on GitHub. It's where you go to download the app, for Mac or Linux.
  • You should see an icon in the browser chrome pointing to Home. Click it to see the home page of dave.writersweb.org. It explains a bit of what's going on, and links to various pages including the Markdown version of Scripting News. That was the first of our test sites, where we figured out how the front matter would make Markdown work with blogging, not just a page of blogging, but a whole site of blog matter. writersweb.org is where Scripting News will be hosted in the BonBonSphere (for lack of a better term) as well as other stuff I write. There will be other similar sites on that domain.
  • Probably the most important step, create your own Hello World page on GitHub and view it in BonBon. Once you see your own Hello World page in BonBon, you'll get the full gestalt of how this works. Short version -- exactly like posting a Hello World page to the historic web, only instead of HTML, it's Markdown. If you're proud of it send me a link. I want to see what people do with it at first.
  • The Bookmarks work, we added some items to the menu to get started, but it's yours to edit and use however you see fit. You can also add bookmarks to the browser chrome.
  • Here's the URL of this post in Markdown. Paste it into the address bar of BB to see how it looks on the other side.
  • If you have questions or comments, the Issues section of the BonBon repo is there for you. Claude can read those notes too. If there are bugs please include info for Claude and I to reproduce the problem. What you did, what you expected to happen, what actually happened.

I will be adding to this page as needed.

I'm really excited to see people using this, especially developers. Remember our mottos: 1. All parts replaceable. 2. Small pieces loosely joined. 3. Writing is so important it deserves its own web.

item.title: Products require showrunners
item.description:
This was a reply to a friend's post on Twitter about how decisions are made in open source communities.

I guess it depends what the goals of the project are.

If you don't have a clear statement of the goals, then you have no means to decide on any specific feature.

I welcome community input on goals, and bug reports and feature requests.

But... the decision belongs to the product showrunner. Try to imagine a great TV series like The Wire or Succession without a showrunner, but rather it was a vote of who showed up one day. It wouldn't fit together with itself as it zigged all across the map.

It's kind of like the US government, never has a working longterm strategy, and is constantly undoing itself.

In the RSS world, as the community leader, I would have listened closely to developers who had skin in the game, a product, either a CMS or feed reader that had a lot of users or who had taken risks in the past that turned into key features for the community. And I would listen for ideas that came from people with no power, because I have missed ideas that came to me that way, the famous near-miss was Adam Curry's "last mile" idea which turned into podcasting. You have to allow an open door for people who see something the rest of us don't.

And every product, open source or not, must be open to competition. So if you don't like what they do, and they won't fix it, then go out and make some news sister or brother. That's how we grow!

But remember to leave the door open for those who follow. Not locked-in, locked-open. :-)

item.title: The danger is real
item.description:
AI has enabled hackers to find security holes in widely deployed software much faster, and it is able to find security holes that humans can’t. So there’s been an until now behind the scenes race by the good guys trying find and fix holes be for the bad guys find and exploit them.

At least some of the recent outages were caused by software that was trying to close security holes that were discovered by AI and the actual code that was doing the updating was AI. Probably the first time it’s ever been called on to do this so it probably didn’t understand all the limits of the networks it was working with. But when you’re dealing with a security issue, there really isn’t a lot of time to consider all the options and sometimes you have to take risks. The system going down isn’t the worst thing that can happen in that context.

The danger is real and our economy, if our computer networks were to fail, would collapse in an instant.

I don’t want to be alarmist, but this is a time to be alarmed because even if we had the best people in the top positions in the government, we would still be in danger.

item.title: My big turn in Claude-land
item.description:
Hopefully this is the last big transition for a while.

I have moved Claude from my Mac Mini to my laptop, which is also my desktop.

Did it very systematically, in a recursive way.

First I asked Claude in the web browser how I should approach this. For me it was essential to put my mind outside either of the two systrems, and I believe it helped set the context for Claude/web.

From there, after coming up with a plan, I got a handoff message from C/W to C/macmini. I opened it and delivered it. And then it was a series of back and forth, looking at each project and looking for problems.

Then C/macmini gave me instructions on how to set up a new Claude app on the laptop, and there were issues, but we went back and forth with help from C/macmini on copying it Claude app from the mini to the laptop.

We're still primarily using C/macmini shouting instructions via my keyboard to C/laptop, and I send back the return, and after a few go-rounds, we're ready for the next step. I picked one of my projects, the one that's most currently my focus -- mdBrowser -- which eventually became BonBon, and asked it to run a script C/mini wrote for me, to ask it to go through tests that reveal any issues.

And that's where I am right now. About 24 hours, with of course time for daily walk in the woods, lunch, dinner, a Knicks game, sleep, coffee and a bit of courage but a lot of awe.

Also realizing that the system I'm running is still in early days. There could be higher level ways of organizing projects, in fact there already are, I haven't incorporated them yet. But this kit made a huge number of things possible that before would have been hit or miss. And the proof is still to come, did it catch all the possible problems?
